input.headline: The flicker of the room's lights matches the national grid record at 11:43:38 UTC on 8 November 2026, within a second of the stated start.
findings: The scene is a dark indoor room lit by ceiling strip lights, with no on-screen clock. The flicker of those lights carried a strong grid signal (69% of the clip usable). The mains hum in the audio was too weak to use.
I searched the whole of 8 November against the national grid record. The best match starts at 11:43:38 UTC (score 0.979). The next-best time that day scored 0.875, well behind.
Matching each half of the video separately puts the start at 11:43:39 and 11:43:37. The two halves agree, so there is no sign of a cut or splice in the timeline.
The best matches on days up to 3 days either side scored no higher than 0.888. A different day is very unlikely.

The match score falls away clearly if the start is moved 10 to 60 seconds either way. The grid record for this date has a reading only every 15 seconds, so the time is precise to a few seconds, not to the exact second.
input.what_it_means: The independent timing evidence supports the stated start of 11:43:37 UTC on Sunday 8 November 2026, and the recording looks like one continuous take. This tells you when the recording was made. It does not tell you who made it or what it shows.
next_steps: If accuracy to the exact second matters, re-run the check against the National Grid operator's (NESO) 1-second record for November 2026 once it is published.
If you need certainty about edits within each half, get the original file from the phone, because this test only checks timing at the level of the two halves.
Weigh this finding alongside the rest of the case evidence.
